book_title: Chapter 3: How It Is Sold & Delivered — Distribution & Unit Economics
title: Sold Direct, Paid by Letter of Credit, Priced by Resin
question: How does Xpro sell and deliver its films and sheets, what controls its costs, and what does a tonne of each product actually earn?

epigraph.quote: In the very, very specialized business, all sales are on LCs.
epigraph.author: Management, Q2 FY2027 earnings call, 4 Nov 2026

web_blocks.takeaway: Of every ₹100 invoiced in FY2026, ₹69.43 went on materials, leaving ₹9.38 of EBITDA, about ₹6.00 before tax and ₹3.87 after tax. Operating cash flow was ₹4.04 per ₹100 against capex of ₹27.82, so free cash flow was negative by ₹23.79 per ₹100 (₹120.24 Cr). That deficit is expansion spending, not operating leakage. About ₹116 Cr of the ₹140.65 Cr capex was the UAE plant, and the rest was the Barjora line and other standalone spending.

web_blocks.title: Who buys, and how the sale is made

web_blocks.html: Xpro sells direct. Its placement document says sales to major industrial customers “are direct through our own marketing teams”, and the managing director said on 30 May 2025: “we are in a B2B segment. We are not in a sell to trade and supply market at all.” [12][41] The price of directness is concentration. From FY2021 to the first nine months of FY2024, the top ten customers were 71.7% to 76.4% of gross revenue [12]. One unnamed customer paid ₹149.41 Cr, or 29.6%, of FY2026 revenue (25.9% in FY2025) [2]. That customer exceeds Xpro's entire dielectric book of ₹135.52 Cr. It must therefore be a refrigerator-sector buyer rather than a capacitor maker (our inference; the company does not name it) [48].

Dielectric film is made to order and qualified customer by customer. Validation “could be anything from zero to many months”, and life tests of 1,000 to 2,000 hours are running at some customers [9][3]. Buyers are only capacitor makers and film metallisers, and “We are selling a film”, not a line's output [9]. Payment is secured because “all sales are on LCs” [3]. A letter of credit (LC) is a bank's promise to pay against shipping documents. No long-term contract, take-or-pay or order book is disclosed. Customer prices are fixed “either annually or for the duration of the agreement” [12]. Sheets and liners go to white-goods OEMs on terms that “generally falls within 120 days” [2]. Standalone receivables of ₹69.22 Cr on ₹505.49 Cr of revenue equal 50 days (our calculation) [2]. Those OEMs can turn rival, as the annual report flags “selective backward integration by certain customers, including under PLI-supported schemes” [2].

web_blocks.title: Raw materials and the supply chain

web_blocks.html: Resin decides the year. Materials cost ₹350.01 Cr, 69.2% of FY2026 revenue (72.2% in FY2025) [2]. Dielectric film needs capacitor-grade polypropylene of “highly specialized, highly specific grades not manufactured in India” [9]. Only three producers make it: Borealis/Borouge, KPIC and TPC. They made about 230,000 t in 2024 against roughly 232,500 t of demand implied for 2025 [43]. A Chinese rival's filing puts resin at 70% to 80% of base-film cost. It says changing supplier takes three months for thick film and about two years for automotive ultra-thin film [46]. Xpro names Borouge and says “a good bit of it comes from the European side”. It has “no long-term agreements with most of our suppliers”, and price and quantity are set per purchase order [3][12]. At that filing's 1.55 t of resin per tonne of film, FY2026's 3,541 t of film needed about 5,500 t of resin, 2.4% of world demand. At 13,000 t the need would be about 20,150 t, or 8.7% (our calculation) [43]. Xpro is a small buyer from a concentrated seller set. Coex resins are bought at home or abroad “as determined by economics” [12].

Stock is the buffer: “we like to make sure we have at least 3 months of stock in the plant” (managing director, 22 May 2026) [9]. Raw-material stock was ₹49.76 Cr at March 2026 against ₹36.74 Cr a year earlier [2]. That is only about 1.7 months of total material use. The three-month rule therefore appears to cover imported specialty grades rather than every input (our calculation and inference).

Pass-through is real but lagged: “Sometimes you get the pass-through contractually, sometimes you have to work on the pass-through. It depends on customer to customer.” Dielectric resin price is not tied to crude because of a “rarity cost”. Coex prices are “more or less directly related to crude” [41]. After resin and freight rose in 2026 the verdict was “the pass-on has been, I will say, not full yet” [3]. Gross margin slid from 30.3% in Q2 FY2026 to 27.5% in Q2 FY2027 on rising revenue [36]. The lag works downward too. When polymer cost fell 10% to 11% in FY2024, dielectric sales fell 6.7% on flat volume (our calculation) [42][21][23].

Machines are the second single point of supply: “for the core line, there is no Chinese alternate” [42]. Only Brückner, Lindauer Dornier and Marchant make capacitor-film lines [46], and commissioning “cannot be less than 2 years today” [3]. Line 2 suffered transit damage in FY2025. West Asia shipping disruption hit 2026 [41][50]. Power and fuel cost ₹26.93 Cr, 5.3% of revenue (our calculation) [2]. Barjora uses DVC grid power and coal-bed methane [2]. Ranjangaon uses open-access solar from the 26%-owned TP Mercury [21]. Power also bit: “recurring external power disruptions slowed the ramp-up” of the new line in Q2 FY2027 [6].

Four plants make the product. Barjora has two dielectric lines of 4,000 t each. Greater Noida and Ranjangaon run seven sheet, seven thermoforming and two cast-film lines. Ras Al Khaimah has one dielectric line commissioning. Group nameplate is 13,000 t of dielectric film, 39,000 t of sheet, 7,000 t of liners and 5,400 t of cast film [2]. Barjora Line 2 was capitalised at ₹212.34 Cr, or ₹5.3 lakh per tonne (₹6.0 lakh on management's “about INR240 crores”). A tonne of capacity sells for ₹3.8 to ₹4.8 lakh a year at full use. Capex is therefore 1.1 to 1.4 times annual sales (our calculation) [2][9].

web_blocks.title: Pricing: what a kilogram of film earns

web_blocks.html: On 4 Nov 2026 management said the “modal price of film is around INR470, INR480 a kilo”, with 3.5 micron “a little over INR600” and 3 micron “near INR900” [3]. On 22 May 2026 it had said “in excess of INR550 a kilo”, adding “I'm just throwing a range” [9]. They differ by about 16% at the midpoint (our calculation). The basis is not stated and the company has not reconciled them, so we treat ₹470 to ₹550 as a band. The audited average is lower. Net sales per kg produced were ₹430, ₹402, ₹383 and ₹383 in FY2023 to FY2026 (our calculation) [2][21][23]. That is 23% to 25% below the November modal price. The thin-gauge ladder is steep: 3.5 micron is about 25% to 28% above modal, and 3 micron about 88% to 91%. Thinner film also cuts tonnes per line-hour [51].

Xpro also chose to cut: “a strategic decision... a slight softening of prices in anticipation of the creation of new capacities” (22 May 2026). The cut was put at 6% to 7% a year earlier [9][41]. On FY2024's ₹145.89 Cr of dielectric revenue that is ₹8.8 Cr to ₹10.2 Cr. That equals 55% to 64% of the ₹15.9 Cr fall in EBITDA into FY2025 (our calculation, full-year effect) [21][16]. A supplier near full utilisation that cuts price to hold customers is behaving as a price taker.

web_blocks.caption: Working-capital days, FY2015 to FY2026 (consolidated; Screener ratios)
web_blocks.takeaway: Suppliers funded the business through FY2022. In FY2026 stocking and faster supplier payment took the cycle to 80 days, a twelve-year high (printed values can differ by a day through rounding).

web_blocks.html: From FY2015 to FY2022 payables averaged 83 days against 58 debtor days and 56 inventory days. The cycle therefore averaged 31 days (our calculation). In FY2026 inventory days rose 19 (57 to 76). Payable days fell 22 (68 to 46) and debtor days fell 3 (our calculation) [32]. There are two causes. Deliberate stocking lifted raw-material stock ₹13.0 Cr, and management tied it on the 4 Nov 2026 call to Hormuz shipping risk [52]. Consolidated payables fell ₹27.6 Cr to ₹43.88 Cr as purchases dropped to ₹363.03 Cr from ₹396.16 Cr [2][8]. Working capital absorbed ₹18.94 Cr in FY2026 (our sum), holding cash from operations to 43% of EBITDA. It absorbed ₹15.7 Cr more in H1 FY2027 as receivables rose about ₹24 Cr on 47% higher revenue. FY2024 to H1 FY2027 absorbed about ₹78 Cr [2][36]. This is the carrying cost of imported resin rather than an earnings-quality flag. Blended debtor days stay near 50 despite LC-backed dielectric, because coex, on credit, is 72% of revenue (our calculation).

In FY2026 dielectric film realised about ₹383/kg against ₹105 for sheet, ₹269 for liners and ₹164 for cast film (our calculation). Even so, it was 11% of reported tonnage and 26.8% of revenue [2].

web_blocks.title: What we conclude, and what is not disclosed
paragraphs: Direct, LC-secured dielectric sales are a real strength. The price is set bilaterally with concentrated buyers, and the FY2025 cut shows who holds the pen. On supply Xpro is a small buyer of resin from three producers and of machines from three builders, with partial pass-through. Group EBITDA per tonne has not been rebuilt (₹26,708 to ₹15,127). The new Barjora line must lift dielectric's share of tonnes, and thin-gauge mix must lift price per kilogram, before economics approach the management ranges.
Not disclosed are segment EBITDA, named dielectric customers, long-term contracts, per-kilogram price history and the new line's tonnes. The dielectric margins above are ranges or back-calculations.

book_paragraphs: Let us start with the simplest question a business can be asked: who writes the cheque, and when? For Xpro India the answer is unusually plain. There is no dealer network, no distributor and no wholesaler in the middle. The placement document says sales to major industrial customers “are direct through our own marketing teams”, and the managing director put it more bluntly on 30 May 2025: “we are in a B2B segment. We are not in a sell to trade and supply market at all.” [12][41] That directness is a double-edged choice. It means no channel margin to share. It also means no cushion, because every rupee comes from a named customer. The top ten customers were between 71.7% and 76.4% of gross revenue in each period from FY2021 to early FY2024, and in FY2026 one customer alone paid ₹149.41 Cr, 29.6% of revenue [12][2].

Can you guess who that customer is? The company will not tell us, but arithmetic points one way. ₹149.41 Cr is more than Xpro's whole dielectric film book of ₹135.52 Cr, so it cannot be a capacitor maker; it is almost certainly a refrigerator maker or a group of them. That is our inference, not a disclosure [2][48]. Keep it in mind, because it tells you which half of the business carries the concentration risk.

Now picture the two halves of the order book. On one side is dielectric film, the thin polypropylene film that sits inside capacitors. Capacitors are the small components that smooth and store electrical energy in fans, inverters, motors and electric-vehicle drives. The buyers are only capacitor makers and the firms that vacuum-coat film with metal, called metallisers [9]. Each buyer tests the film in its own way. The managing director said validation “could be anything from zero to many months”, and capacitor life tests of 1,000 to 2,000 hours are running at some customers today [9][3]. Nothing is made for stock: the product is “produced against confirmed requirements, designed in consultation with the customers” [42].

And how do they pay? Here is the line I want you to underline: “In the very, very specialized business, all sales are on LCs.” [3] An LC, a letter of credit, is a bank's promise to pay the seller once the shipping papers are in order. It turns a customer's promise into a bank's promise. No long-term contract, no take-or-pay clause and no order-book value is disclosed, and the placement document says customer prices are fixed “either annually or for the duration of the agreement” [12]. So the security is in the payment, not in a locked-in volume.

The other half is plastic sheet and moulded refrigerator liners from Greater Noida and Ranjangaon, sold to white-goods makers on open credit, with terms that “generally falls within 120 days” [2]. Standalone receivables of ₹69.22 Cr on ₹505.49 Cr of revenue work out to about 50 days (our calculation). Add cast films for tyre release and hygiene products, and exports of just ₹22.45 Cr, 4.4% of revenue, mostly dielectric to the United States and Germany and sheet to Sri Lanka [2]. Notice something uncomfortable: the annual report itself warns of “selective backward integration by certain customers, including under PLI-supported schemes” [2]. Your biggest customer may be thinking about becoming your competitor.

Turn now to what goes into the film. Resin is the cost that decides the year: ₹350.01 Cr of materials, 69.2% of FY2026 revenue [2]. The capacitor-grade polypropylene is, in management's words, “highly specialized, highly specific grades not manufactured in India, even though India is a large polypropylene resin producer, that is mainly packaging types” [9]. Worldwide, three producers make it: Borealis and Borouge, KPIC of Korea and TPC of Singapore [43]. Xpro names Borouge as a supplier and says much arrives from Europe [3]. It has no long-term agreements with most suppliers; price and quantity are settled order by order [12].

How big a customer is Xpro to those three? Using a Chinese rival's rule of thumb of 1.55 t of resin per tonne of film, FY2026's 3,541 t of film needed about 5,500 t of resin, 2.4% of world demand. At 13,000 t of film that rises to about 20,150 t, or 8.7% (our calculation) [43]. It is a small buyer facing a few sellers, so we should not assume it can bargain. Management's answer is stock: “at any point of time, this being an imported raw material, we like to make sure we have at least 3 months of stock in the plant” [9]. By our arithmetic the whole raw-material pile is only about 1.7 months of consumption, so the three-month rule seems to apply to the specialty grades, not to every input.

What happens when resin moves? Management is candid: “Sometimes you get the pass-through contractually, sometimes you have to work on the pass-through. It depends on customer to customer.” [41] After the West Asia conflict lifted resin and freight, the verdict was that “the pass-on has been, I will say, not full yet” [3]. You can see it in gross margin, which slid from 30.3% to 27.5% across a year of rising sales [36]. The lag also works downward. When polymer cost fell 10% to 11% in FY2024, dielectric sales fell 6.7% on flat tonnage [42][21][23]. The machines are the other bottleneck: for the core line there is “no Chinese alternate”, only three European builders, and commissioning “cannot be less than 2 years today” [42][46][3].

Now the part every analyst wants and the company declines to give: what does a kilogram sell for? In November 2026 the “modal price of film is around INR470, INR480 a kilo”, with 3.5 micron film at a little over ₹600 and 3 micron near ₹900 [3]. Six months earlier the same range was “in excess of INR550 a kilo”, offered with the caveat “I'm just throwing a range” [9]. The audited average is lower than both: ₹383 per kilogram in FY2026, down from ₹430 in FY2023 (our calculation) [2][23]. So treat the quoted prices as an indicative band, not a data series.

That price decline was partly a decision. “We had taken a strategic decision and had worked towards a slight softening of prices in anticipation of the creation of new capacities.” [9] On FY2024's dielectric revenue, a 6% to 7% cut is worth ₹8.8 Cr to ₹10.2 Cr, more than half of the ₹15.9 Cr fall in group EBITDA that year (our calculation) [21][16]. Warren Buffett told the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission in 2010 that “the single most important decision in evaluating a business is pricing power”. A company that cuts price while running near full capacity, to pre-empt competitors, has told you something about how much of it it has.

Next, the cash cycle. Look at the history: from FY2015 to FY2022 suppliers were paid slowly, around 83 days on average, so they financed the business and the cycle from paying for raw material to collecting from customers averaged 31 days. In FY2026 it reached 80 days. Inventory days went from 57 to 76, payable days from 68 to 46, and debtor days from 53 to 50 [32]. Management explained the stocking: “if I can buy and stock for 3 months, I would”, tied to shipping risk through Hormuz [52]. Meanwhile payables fell ₹27.6 Cr as purchases shrank [2][8]. The result was that working capital absorbed ₹18.94 Cr, and cash from operations was only 43% of EBITDA [2]. Add ₹15.7 Cr more in the first half of FY2027 as receivables rose on 47% higher sales [36]. It is the real carrying cost of importing a specialty resin, not an accounting trick.

Now follow the money on a single rupee. Take ₹100 of FY2026 revenue. Materials took ₹69.43, employees ₹7.44 and other operating costs ₹13.75, leaving ₹9.38 of EBITDA. Depreciation took ₹2.37, interest ₹1.49, and a small net other income of ₹0.48 left about ₹6.00 before tax and ₹3.87 after tax. Cash from operations was ₹4.04, but capex was ₹27.82, so free cash flow was a negative ₹23.79 [2]. That is not leakage. About ₹116 Cr of the ₹140.65 Cr capex was the UAE plant, and the rest was the Barjora line and other standalone spending. Note, too, that other income of ₹18.21 Cr was almost wiped out by a ₹15.78 Cr foreign-exchange loss on the euro loans, mostly unrealised, so ₹2.43 Cr remained [2].

Now the comparison I promised, built only from management's own ranges and so purely illustrative. Imagine a ₹100 invoice for dielectric film and another for refrigerator sheet. Management says dielectric EBITDA runs 35% to 55% and coex 5% to 7% [3]. So the dielectric invoice keeps ₹35 to ₹55 and the sheet invoice keeps ₹5 to ₹7. But backing the coex range out of reported FY2026 EBITDA leaves dielectric at roughly 16% to 23%, not 35% to 55% (our calculation). Even at that lower figure, a tonne of dielectric earns roughly 8 to 17 times the EBITDA of a tonne of sheet. You need about 114 to 163 tonnes of film to earn ₹1 Cr of EBITDA, against about 1,357 to 1,899 tonnes of sheet.

That is why the unit economics matter more than the headline sales. Group EBITDA per tonne fell from ₹26,708 in FY2023 to ₹15,127 in FY2026 while tonnes rose 12.5%, because the new tonnes were mostly sheet (our calculation). The extra Barjora line is supposed to reverse that. It must lift dielectric's share of tonnes, and thin-gauge films must lift the price per kilogram, before group economics resemble the management ranges. What is not disclosed is just as important: no segment profit, no named dielectric customers, no long-term contracts, no per-kilogram price history. We have ranges and back-calculations, and we should say so.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A business can be secured at the point of payment and still be exposed at the point of price. Xpro's letters of credit mean it rarely worries about being paid for dielectric film; the FY2025 price cut, the three resin suppliers and the incomplete pass-through of resin cost show how little it controls on either side of the sale. Track the gap between what customers pay per kilogram and what resin costs per kilogram, because that spread, not the revenue line, is where the unit economics live.
